traveler: Agustí Querol i Subirats (Agustín Querol Subirats)
title: The Baker's Son: Dough, Marble, and the Monuments Spain Shipped Across the Ocean
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Tortosa, birth in the baker's house
stops.date_confidence: attested; both the Catalan and English Wikipedia articles give 17 May 1860
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of May a son is born to a baker of Tortosa, in the Baix Ebre, where the river runs wide toward the delta. The father comes from Ulldecona and keeps an oven; the house smells of flour and heat, and the boy grows up inside the trade he is expected to inherit. His biographer Rodolfo Gil will describe him small before the fired oven, his fingers working the leaven, pinching scraps of dough into little figures. The first modelling he does is in bread, and nobody in Tortosa reads it as anything but a child playing with his hands.
stops.quote: Niño aún, en su hogar humilde y ante el horno caldeado, su vocación nativa despierta y sus dedos inquietos y tiernos hiñen la levadura y con trozos de masa ensayan su afición en graciosas figurillas.
stops.quote_source: Rodolfo Gil, 'Agustín Querol', Madrid, Sáenz de Jubera Hermanos, 1910, biographical section on his origins
suggested_refs: The bakers' quarter of old Tortosa on the right bank of the Ebro

stops.name: Tortosa, the first master
stops.date_confidence: undated in sources; placed in boyhood, before the departure for Barcelona at eighteen
stops.campa: Ramon Cerveto Bestraten, founder of a dynasty of Tortosa artists, takes the baker's son as a pupil and gives him his first instruction in drawing and modelling. The town has no academy; what it has is a workshop, a master with local commissions, and a boy who has already learned that a soft material holds whatever shape a hand leaves in it. Under Cerveto the play with dough becomes a discipline with clay, and the oven loses its claim on him. His father will not get the baker he expected to raise.
suggested_refs: The workshop of Ramon Cerveto Bestraten, first of the Cerveto artists of Tortosa

segments.name: Barcelona: the Llotja and the Dissection Room

stops.name: Barcelona, arrival at eighteen
stops.date_confidence: inferred; sources state his age as eighteen rather than the year, so 1878 follows from the 1860 birth
stops.campa: At eighteen he leaves the bakery for good and goes up to Barcelona, a city rebuilding itself outside its demolished walls and hungry for stone carvers and for men who can model a saint onto a facade. He arrives with a provincial master's training and no money behind him. The Escola Provincial de Belles Arts, lodged in the old Llotja de Mar beside the harbour, takes students who can draw; the workshops of the growing Eixample take hands that can work. He enters both. He will not live in Tortosa again.
suggested_refs: The Llotja de Mar of Barcelona, seat of the Escola Provincial de Belles Arts

stops.name: Barcelona, the studios of Talarn and the Vallmitjana brothers
stops.date_confidence: undated in sources; placed within the Barcelona apprenticeship, roughly 1878 to 1884
stops.campa: He apprentices in the studio of Domènec Talarn, master of polychrome religious imagery, and then with the brothers Agapit and Venanci Vallmitjana, who between them hold most of the monumental sculpture in Catalonia. In their workshops he learns the industrial side of the art: the armature, the clay sketch, the plaster cast, the pointing machine, the marble cut by assistants from a model the master never touches with a chisel. It is the method he will run in Madrid at a scale no Spanish studio has attempted.
suggested_refs: The Vallmitjana brothers' workshop, the dominant sculpture studio of nineteenth-century Barcelona

stops.name: Barcelona, the dissection room of the Hospital de la Santa Creu
stops.date_confidence: undated in sources; placed within the Barcelona apprenticeship, roughly 1878 to 1884
stops.campa: Not satisfied with the academy's plaster casts, he enrols in dissection at the Hospital de la Santa Creu and studies anatomy on the bodies themselves. Sculptors of his generation are taught the figure from the antique; he wants it from the inside, the origin and insertion of every muscle under the skin he will later have to carve. The habit shows in the work afterward: the strained neck of an allegory, the tendon standing in a forearm, bronze that behaves like flesh because he has seen what is under it. He learns the figure from the cadaver and the chisel from the workshop in the same years.
suggested_refs: The anatomy theatre of the Hospital de la Santa Creu, Raval, Barcelona

stops.name: Barcelona, the Cabeza de Dolorosa
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by the English Wikipedia article; no month given
stops.campa: He makes a Cabeza de Dolorosa, a head of the Mother of Sorrows, in the devotional line his master Talarn worked all his life. It is among the first pieces to leave his own hands under his own name, a young sculptor proving he can do what the church market asks. The grief in it is conventional and the execution is not. Barcelona notices him a little, and the notice is enough to keep him in clay for another year. He is twenty-one, and everything he has made so far has been made for someone else's altar.
suggested_refs: Cabeza de Dolorosa, 1881, among Querol's earliest recorded works

stops.name: Barcelona, the clay Theodorini
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by the Catalan Wikipedia article; no month given
stops.campa: The Romanian soprano Elena Theodorini sings in Barcelona and he models her in clay. It is not a commission from a church or a facade contractor but a sculptor's own choice of subject, a living woman famous for a voice, taken from the theatre rather than the missal. The opera houses of the city are where a young artist goes to see the century's own faces. It is the first work in his catalogue whose subject is alive and standing in front of him, and he will go on preferring faces his own century can recognise.
suggested_refs: The Barcelona opera seasons of the early 1880s, in which Elena Theodorini sang

stops.name: Madrid, the pension won
stops.date_confidence: year attested across the Spanish, English and Catalan articles; no month given, and the coordinate is a central-Madrid pin, not a documented address
stops.campa: He competes for the state pension that sends Spanish sculptors to Rome and wins it, together with Eduardo Barrón. The pension is the ladder the Spanish system provides: years in Italy at government expense, with obligatory works sent home to prove the money is not wasted. For a baker's son from the Ebro it is the passage out of the provincial workshop into the official career. He comes to Madrid to compete and leaves for Italy carrying an appointment that makes him, at twenty-four, a sculptor of the state.
suggested_refs: The competitive pensions for sculpture at the Real Academia de España en Roma

stops.name: Rome, the Real Academia on the Janiculum
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month not attested and defaulted
stops.campa: The Real Academia de España keeps its pensioners on the Janiculum, above Trastevere, at San Pietro in Montorio. Here the Spaniards of his year draw from the antique in the mornings and from Rome itself the rest of the day: the Laocoön, the Barberini Faun, Bernini's marble that behaves like cloth and like skin. Querol arrives out of a Catalan workshop where sculpture meant contracts and scaffolding, and finds an art with two thousand years of its own behind it. He stays several years, drawing the antique and sending the obligatory works home to Madrid.
suggested_refs: The Real Academia de España en Roma at San Pietro in Montorio, Janiculum

stops.name: Rome, the bust of Eduard Toda and the Sagunto
stops.date_confidence: the Toda bust is attributed to 1885 and the Sagunto to 1886; sources do not say whether the Sagunto was modelled in Rome or in Madrid
stops.campa: He cuts a portrait bust of Eduard Toda i Güell, the Catalan diplomat and archaeologist who opened tombs in Egypt and will one day rebuild the monastery of Poblet; it goes to the Biblioteca Museu Víctor Balaguer at Vilanova. In the same years he produces Sagunto, on the Iberian city that burned itself rather than fall to Hannibal, the piece that will end in the Museo del Prado. Portraiture pays for the pension years; the historical subject is what a Spanish jury rewards. He has found the second one, and he will not leave it again.
suggested_refs: The bust of Eduard Toda at the Biblioteca Museu Víctor Balaguer, Vilanova i la Geltrú

stops.name: Madrid, La Tradición and the first-class medal
stops.date_confidence: year attested across three language editions; no month given
stops.campa: La Tradición takes a first-class medal at the Exposición Nacional de Bellas Artes in Madrid, the award that certifies a Spanish artist to the state and to every town council with a monument to raise. The bronze afterwards enters the Prado. He is twenty-seven, a few years out of the Vallmitjana workshop, and the machinery of official commissions begins to turn toward him. After this medal the commissions arrive faster than one pair of hands can model them, which is how the studio he opens later comes to hold dozens.
suggested_refs: La Tradición, bronze, Museo Nacional del Prado

stops.name: Barcelona, first prize at the Universal Exposition
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the Catalan Wikipedia article; no month given
stops.campa: Barcelona clears the old citadel and throws its Universal Exposition across the Parc de la Ciutadella, the city announcing itself to Europe in iron, brick, and sculpture. Querol takes first prize. The exposition is the ceremony of a bourgeoisie that intends to commission monuments for the next thirty years, and it hands its highest sculptural honour to a man of twenty-eight out of Tortosa. Catalan work follows at once, beginning with the cathedral itself.
suggested_refs: The 1888 Exposición Universal de Barcelona in the Parc de la Ciutadella

stops.name: Barcelona Cathedral, Sant Feliu and Santa Eulàlia
stops.date_confidence: year attested across three language editions; no month given
stops.campa: The cathedral of Barcelona is finishing the neo-Gothic front its medieval builders never raised, and Querol carves for it Sant Feliu and Santa Eulàlia: the martyr of Girona and the girl the city keeps in its crypt, thirteen years old, killed under Diocletian and remembered rolled down a street in a barrel of knives. He is set to work in a style five centuries older than himself and made to disappear inside it. The stone goes up among hundreds of figures, unsigned to anyone looking from the square below.
suggested_refs: The neo-Gothic facade of the Cathedral of Santa Eulàlia, Barcelona

stops.name: Vigo, the admiral of Callao
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the Spanish Wikipedia works list names Vigo as the city, but the coordinate is an approximate plaza pin and the original siting within Vigo is unconfirmed
stops.campa: Vigo raises a monument to Casto Méndez Núñez, the admiral who took the Spanish squadron against the batteries of Callao in 1866 and was remembered for preferring honour without ships to ships without honour. Querol makes it. The commission is the first of the type that will occupy the rest of his life: a provincial city, a public subscription, a naval or civil hero, bronze on a pedestal in a square. Spain, losing what remains of its empire, builds these faster than it builds anything else.
suggested_refs: The Monumento a Méndez Núñez, Vigo

segments.name: The Studio on the Paseo del Cisne

stops.name: Madrid, the studio on the paseo del Cisne
stops.date_confidence: both the English and Spanish articles put him in Madrid from 1890; the coordinate is that of the paseo de Eduardo Dato, formerly paseo del Cisne, not a documented house number
stops.campa: He leaves Rome for Madrid and opens a studio on the paseo del Cisne, in Chamberí, the street later renamed for Eduardo Dato. It is not a studio in the romantic sense but a works: dozens of assistants, modellers, marble cutters, and pointers, running several monumental commissions at once for cities on two continents. Lorenzo Coullaut Valera and Jacinto Higueras pass through it, and dozens more. For twenty years a great part of Spain's public sculpture, wherever it ends up standing, leaves from this address.
stops.quote: Nos hallamos en un período de transición; vivimos en una época crítica para el arte. Unos miran al pasado con amor ferviente... amo el pasado lleno de encanto y de hermosura; pero, como hombre de este siglo, tengo fe en los adelantos de las artes.
stops.quote_source: Querol's stated credo, quoted in Rodolfo Gil, 'Agustín Querol', Madrid, Sáenz de Jubera Hermanos, 1910, p. 5, introduced by Gil with 'Y así lo confiesa'
suggested_refs: The Querol studio on the paseo del Cisne, today paseo de Eduardo Dato, Chamberí, Madrid

stops.name: Munich, the gold medals
stops.date_confidence: the 1891 and 1895 Munich golds are attested to the year; no source consulted places Querol himself in Munich, only his sculpture
stops.campa: His work is sent to the international exhibition at Munich and takes a gold medal; four years later it takes a second. German juries are judging a Spaniard who arrived by way of a Catalan workshop and a Roman pension, and they read in him what the period wants read: technical mastery in the service of large public feeling. The medals travel back to Madrid ahead of him, and so does the reputation. By mid-decade his is one of the two names, with Mariano Benlliure's, that Spanish letters use as shorthand for monumental sculpture.
stops.quote: Pues es necesario animarles a que la erijan, y a que den el encargo a un Querol o un Benlliure... Ya verá usted el partido que saben sacar cualquiera de estos dos escultores de esa poética leyenda del amor y la abnegación, verdaderamente sobrehumanos.
stops.quote_source: Nicasio Mariscal, 'Posfación a las Memorias Íntimas', in Obras Completas de Eusebio Blasco, tomo IV
suggested_refs: The Münchener Internationale Kunstausstellung of 1891 and 1895
sources: Nicasio Mariscal, in Obras Completas de Eusebio Blasco IV (Wikisource)

stops.name: Madrid, the Museo de Arte Moderno
stops.date_confidence: the vice-directorship is attested for 1892 and given as running to 1895; the coordinate is that of the Palacio de Biblioteca y Museos Nacionales, which housed the museum
stops.campa: He is made vice-director of the Museo de Arte Moderno, installed with the national library in the Palacio de Biblioteca y Museos Nacionales on the paseo de Recoletos. The post puts him inside the institution that decides which living Spanish artists the state buys, at the moment when he is the living Spanish sculptor the state buys most. He holds it three years. In the same years he deals in Carrara marble and writes for the press under a pseudonym, El Plutarco del Pueblo.
suggested_refs: The Museo de Arte Moderno de Madrid in the Palacio de Biblioteca y Museos Nacionales

stops.name: Vigo, the Elduayen monument
stops.date_confidence: 1896 in the Querol biography article, 1897 in the Spanish Wikipedia works list; contested and unresolved. The monument stands in the Jardines de Elduayen, Vigo, but the coordinate here is unsourced
stops.campa: Vigo commissions him a second time, now for José Elduayen, marquis of Pazo de la Merced, minister and deputy for the city, whose name the gardens above the old town still carry. The formula is the one the century has settled on: a standing bronze, a marble pedestal, an inscription, a subscription list of local names. Querol supplies it from Madrid without needing to see the square. A monument in this period is a manufactured object, ordered from a studio the way a bridge is ordered from a foundry.
suggested_refs: The Monumento a José Elduayen in the Jardines de Elduayen, Vigo, pedestal by Jenaro de la Fuente Domínguez
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Jenaro de la Fuente Domínguez'

stops.name: Barcelona, Moses and the Laws for the Palace of Justice
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the Catalan Wikipedia article; the coordinate is the Palau de Justícia on the passeig de Lluís Companys and is not taken from a source that gives coordinates
stops.campa: For the Palau de Justícia rising on the passeig de Lluís Companys he carves Moisès i les lleis, Moses with the tablets, the lawgiver set over the courts of a city that has just written itself a modern legal order. The prophet who came down from Sinai with the law cut into stone is the natural patron of a building where law is applied, and Querol gives him the beard, the arm, and the anger of the Renaissance version everyone already knows. Catalan jurisprudence is guarded in the idiom of Rome.
suggested_refs: Moisès i les lleis, Palau de Justícia de Barcelona

stops.name: Madrid, La Gloria y los Pegasos
stops.date_confidence: contested: 1897 in the Spanish Wikipedia biography, 1897-1902 in the Catalan article, 1905 in the dedicated Spanish article on La Gloria y los Pegasos. Not resolved. The building is the Palacio de Fomento, only later the Ministry of Agriculture
stops.campa: For the enormous Palacio de Fomento at Atocha he models La Gloria y los Pegasos, winged horses reined by allegorical figures along the roofline, the heaviest bronze group in the city. Glory rides above the ministry of public works, over the railways, the roads, and the harbour engineering of a state that is losing an empire and building a country. He works it at a scale that needs a foundry and a small army, which is what the paseo del Cisne has become. Whatever else Madrid forgets of him, it keeps the Pegasos.
suggested_refs: La Gloria y los Pegasos, Palacio de Fomento, Madrid
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'La Gloria y los Pegasos'

stops.name: Vienna, the gold medal
stops.date_confidence: year attested across three language editions; as with Munich, no source places Querol himself in the city, only his work
stops.campa: A gold medal comes from Vienna in the year Spain loses the war with the United States and signs away Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines. Abroad his allegories are read as accomplished European sculpture. At home, in the year of the Disaster, every allegory of glory, tradition, and fatherland is read as an argument. The decade in which Spain stops being an empire is the decade it orders monuments hardest, and the orders go to the paseo del Cisne.
stops.quote_source: Arsenio Alexandre, French critic, quoted among the opening epigraphs of Rodolfo Gil, 'Agustín Querol', Madrid, 1910, p. 3; Gil gives no further bibliographic detail
suggested_refs: The 1898 Vienna international art exhibition

stops.name: Madrid, the front of the Biblioteca Nacional
stops.date_confidence: the commission is given as running roughly 1892 to 1903; 1903 is the completion year and stands here for the whole. A claim that the group numbers nineteen figures is not supported by the sources consulted
stops.campa: Across eleven years he cuts the sculpture of the Biblioteca Nacional's front on the paseo de Recoletos, the pediment group and the crowning figure of Spain above the whole facade. It is his longest single commission, and the one most Madrileños walk past without knowing whose it is. The state's own library is sculpted by the state's own sculptor, and the figure of Spain goes up over the door in the years the country is explaining to itself what it has just lost.
stops.quote: Artista pensador, hombre que conoce el pasado y aspira a dominar el porvenir.
stops.quote_source: Delahaye, quoted among the opening epigraphs of Rodolfo Gil, 'Agustín Querol', Madrid, 1910, p. 3; Gil gives no further bibliographic detail
suggested_refs: The pediment and crowning figure of the Biblioteca Nacional de España, paseo de Recoletos

segments.name: Bronzes Shipped to Cities He Never Saw

stops.name: Manila, Intramuros: Legazpi and Urdaneta
stops.date_confidence: the Spanish Wikipedia works list dates the monument 1893; its erection in Manila was authorised in 1901. An earlier account that American sculptors completed it is contradicted by the dedicated Spanish article, which credits the bronzes to Querol
stops.campa: He casts in Barcelona the bronzes of the Monumento a Legazpi y Urdaneta, the conquistador who took the islands for Philip II and the Augustinian friar who found the return route across the Pacific, and the finished work is shipped to Manila. He never sets foot in the Philippines. By the time the monument is authorised to rise in Intramuros the archipelago is no longer Spanish and the officer signing the permission is an American provost marshal. The bronze commemorates a conquest that has just ended.
suggested_refs: The Monumento a Legazpi y Urdaneta, Intramuros, Manila, architect Luis María Cabello
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Monumento a Legazpi y Urdaneta'

stops.name: Havana, the firemen of the Necrópolis de Colón
stops.date_confidence: commissioned 1892, inaugurated 1897; both years attested. Querol is not attested to have travelled to Havana
stops.campa: In the Necrópolis de Colón at Havana his Monumento a los Bomberos is unveiled, raised over the firemen killed in the great fire of 1890, marble and bronze piled among the mausoleums with an angel above and a mourning figure below. It is designed in Madrid, cast in Spain, and shipped across the Atlantic to a colony with one year of Spanish rule left in it. Cuban Havana keeps it and goes on burying its dead around it long after the flag it was made under has come down.
suggested_refs: The Monumento a los Bomberos, Necrópolis de Cristóbal Colón, Havana

stops.name: Mexico City, the Pegasos of the Palacio de Bellas Artes
stops.date_confidence: no source consulted dates the Bellas Artes groups precisely; the span c.1904-1909 is taken from the building's construction years, so the date shown is approximate
stops.campa: Porfirio Díaz is building Mexico a national theatre of Italian marble on the edge of the Alameda, and the commission for its Pegasos, winged horses for the exterior, reaches the studio on the paseo del Cisne. Querol works them for a building he will not see finished: the revolution stops the construction, and the Palacio de Bellas Artes will not open for another thirty years. His horses wait through it. He casts the same animal and the same allegory for a president in Mexico that he cast for a ministry in Madrid.
suggested_refs: The Pegasos of the Palacio de Bellas Artes, Mexico City

stops.name: Lima, Plaza Bolognesi
stops.date_confidence: designed 1902, inaugurated 6 November 1905; both attested
stops.campa: Lima unveils his Monumento al coronel Francisco Bolognesi, the officer who held Arica against the Chileans to the last cartridge. Querol shows him at the end, head bowed, gripping the flagstaff, a hero in the instant of defeat rather than of victory. Peru objects; Manuel González Prada among others calls the pose undignified for a man who died fighting. In 1954 the government takes it down for a Bolognesi with his sword raised, and Querol's original goes to the fortress museum of the Real Felipe.
suggested_refs: Querol's original Bolognesi, Museo Histórico Militar del Real Felipe, Callao
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Plaza Bolognesi' and 'Monumento a Bolognesi'

segments.name: Marble, the Cortes, and the Sieges

stops.name: Madrid, the seated Claudio Moyano
stops.date_confidence: inaugurated 11 November 1900 per the dedicated Spanish article; the Querol biography article gives 1899, a discrepancy resolved here in favour of the dedicated article
stops.campa: Madrid unveils his seated Claudio Moyano at the foot of the slope beside the Jardín Botánico, the minister who in 1857 wrote the law that made primary schooling in Spain compulsory and free. The bookstalls that will one day line the hill behind him do not exist yet. Querol gives him a chair, a book, and the heavy calm of a man legislating. A country that has spent a decade raising monuments to its lost admirals raises one, at last, to a schoolmaster's statute.
suggested_refs: The Monumento a Claudio Moyano, Plaza del Emperador Carlos V, Madrid

stops.name: Madrid, the Gran Cruz de Alfonso XII
stops.date_confidence: year attested across three language editions; no month given, and the coordinate is the royal palace as a civic pin rather than a documented site of the award
stops.campa: The crown gives him the Gran Cruz de la Orden Civil de Alfonso XII, the highest civil decoration for services to education and the arts. He is forty-two. The baker's son from Tortosa is a decorated man of the state, running the studio that supplies its monuments, holding a museum post, dealing in Carrara marble, and shortly to sit in its parliament. In private, his biographer records, he calls the public part of it the art of pitifully wasting time, and says he cannot spare an instant.
stops.quote: La política, decía en la intimidad con cierto dejo de amargura, es el arte de perder lastimosamente el tiempo, y yo no puedo perder un instante.
stops.quote_source: Rodolfo Gil, 'Agustín Querol', Madrid, Sáenz de Jubera Hermanos, 1910, p. 16, reporting a private remark
suggested_refs: The Orden Civil de Alfonso XII, instituted 1902 for merit in education and the arts

stops.name: Madrid, the Quevedo monument unveiled
stops.date_confidence: inaugurated 5 June 1902 in the Plaza de Alonso Martínez; the coordinate is the Glorieta de Quevedo, where the monument was moved in the 1960s and where it stands now
stops.campa: For the coming of age of Alfonso XIII, Madrid unveils his monument to Francisco de Quevedo in the Plaza de Alonso Martínez: the satirist, the spectacles, the man who wrote the sharpest Spanish of the seventeenth century and died in disgrace for it. Sixty years later the city moves him to the glorieta that already carries his name. A court celebrates a boy king's majority by putting up in bronze the writer who told the seventeenth century exactly what its court was worth.
suggested_refs: The Monumento a Quevedo, Glorieta de Quevedo, Madrid, originally Plaza de Alonso Martínez

stops.name: Zaragoza, the martyrs in the Plaza de España
stops.date_confidence: contested: 1904 in the Spanish Wikipedia biography, 1906 in the Catalan article and in the dedicated Spanish article on the monument. Not resolved; the coordinate is the Plaza de España, Zaragoza, and is not taken from a source giving coordinates
stops.campa: With the architect Ricardo Magdalena he raises in the Plaza de España the Monumento a los mártires de la religión y de la patria, to the priests and civilians killed when the French came against the city a century before. Zaragoza is preparing the centenary of 1808 and wants its dead in stone before the anniversary arrives. Querol gets the martyrs first and the great monument to the sieges afterward. The city hires him twice to say one thing in two registers.
suggested_refs: The Monumento a los mártires de la religión y de la patria, Plaza de España, Zaragoza
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Monumento a los mártires de la religión y de la patria'

stops.name: Madrid, the mausoleum of Cánovas del Castillo
stops.date_confidence: contested across four sources: 1903 in the Catalan article, 1906 in the English article and in the dedicated Spanish article on the Panteón, 1908 in the Spanish biography. The dedicated article's 1906 is followed here and the spread left unresolved
stops.campa: In the Panteón de Hombres Ilustres beside the basilica of Atocha he carves the tomb of Antonio Cánovas del Castillo, architect of the Restoration monarchy, shot dead by an Italian anarchist at a spa in 1897. The mausoleum runs eight metres wide and seven high in white marble, the largest thing in the pantheon. He is by now the sculptor the Spanish state calls when it must bury a prime minister, and here he carves the man who designed the system that has employed him his whole career.
suggested_refs: The Cánovas del Castillo mausoleum, Panteón de Hombres Ilustres, Madrid

stops.name: Bilbao, the park of the widow of Epalza
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the English article names the work as a monument to Casilda Iturrizar, the Spanish works list as a monument to the widow of Epalza, the same woman under two designations
stops.campa: Bilbao commissions a monument to Casilda Iturrizar, widow of Epalza, who left her fortune to the city for schools and charity and whose name the great park of the Ensanche now carries. Querol makes her in the same year he is making the Cánovas tomb and the Barcelona playwright, one more figure out of the same studio. Iron Bilbao commemorates neither a soldier nor a minister but a woman who gave money away, and sets her at the centre of the green ground her bequest paid for.
suggested_refs: The Monumento a Casilda Iturrizar, Parque de Doña Casilda Iturrizar, Bilbao
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Parque de Doña Casilda Iturrizar'

stops.name: Barcelona, the Pitarra monument on the Rambla
stops.date_confidence: inaugurated 26 December 1906 in the Plaça del Teatre, with the mayor Domènec Sanllehy presiding; a claim that Soler's son Ernest gave the inaugural address is not supported by the dedicated article and is not carried here
stops.campa: By public subscription and with the architect Pere Falqués, Barcelona unveils at the low end of the Rambla his monument to Frederic Soler, the watchmaker who under the name Serafí Pitarra wrote Catalan comedy back into existence and filled the theatres of this very square. The mayor Domènec Sanllehy presides. Querol, who left this city for Rome and Madrid twenty years before, returns to it in bronze, at the place where Catalan was spoken from a stage before it was permitted in print.
suggested_refs: The Monumento a Frederic Soler, Plaça del Teatre, La Rambla, Barcelona

stops.name: Roquetes, elected to the Cortes
stops.date_confidence: the term is given as running April 1907 to April 1910; the day is not attested and is defaulted, and the coordinate marks the town centre with no building specified
stops.campa: He is elected deputy to the Cortes for the district of Roquetes, the town beside his native Tortosa, on the Conservative benches. The Ebro sends its baker's son to Madrid a second time, now with a seat. He keeps the studio at full output through the legislature; the commissions do not slow and neither does he. In the chamber he sits among the men whose monuments he has carved, or has been asked to carve, or will be asked to carve for their tombs. The term is to run three years. He will not finish it.
suggested_refs: The Conservative benches of the Cortes, legislature of 1907-1910, district of Roquetes

stops.name: Zaragoza, Plaza de los Sitios
stops.date_confidence: inaugurated 28 October 1908; the bronzes were installed the following year
stops.campa: Alfonso XIII presides at the unveiling of the Monumento a los Sitios, for the centenary of the two sieges Zaragoza held against the French. The bronzes are not ready. The Ballarín foundry has fallen behind, and plaster stand-ins painted the colour of copper take their places for the ceremony; the real figures come by train only eight days before the Pilar festivities of the following year. Querol writes afterward to Segismundo Moret about what he had wanted the thing to be, and what stone and bronze will not do.
stops.quote: Quisiera realizar un imposible: juntar dos montañas por su cima, formar con los hombres y las cosas, con sus pasiones, la espiral de la Historia que eleva a la redención; pero en la lucha por dar vida y animación a la piedra y el bronce, por mucho que el arte ayude, queda la materia más acá del ensueño.
stops.quote_source: Querol to Segismundo Moret after the 1908 inauguration of the Monumento a los Sitios, quoted in Rodolfo Gil, 'Agustín Querol', Madrid, 1910, p. 7
suggested_refs: The Monumento a los Sitios, Plaza de los Sitios, Zaragoza

segments.name: The Gift to Argentina and the End

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Palermo: the gift designed
stops.date_confidence: contested: the English article dates the design to 1900, another summary gives 1909-1910 for design and donation. The cornerstone was laid in 1910. Not resolved
stops.campa: The Spanish community of Argentina, rich, numerous, and preparing a gift for the centenary of the May Revolution, commissions the Monumento a la Carta Magna y las Cuatro Regiones Argentinas, to stand where the Avenida del Libertador meets the Avenida Sarmiento in Palermo. Liberty on top; Peace, Justice, and Agriculture below; four bronzes for the Andes, the Río de la Plata, the Pampa, and the Chaco around a basin. He designs the whole of it from Madrid, for a country he has never crossed the ocean to see.
stops.quote: la confraternidad de españoles y argentinos por la comunidad de sangre y aspiraciones y por la unidad de espíritu é idioma
stops.quote_source: Rodolfo Gil, 'Agustín Querol', Madrid, Sáenz de Jubera Hermanos, 1910, p. 41, on the idea behind the monument; quoted mid-sentence and lowercase as printed
suggested_refs: The Monumento a la Carta Magna y las Cuatro Regiones Argentinas, Palermo, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Madrid, death in the fiftieth year
stops.date_confidence: death in Madrid on 14 December 1909 attested across three language editions; no source gives an address, so the studio pin on the paseo de Eduardo Dato stands in
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of December he dies in Madrid, forty-nine years old, five months short of fifty. The Buenos Aires monument is unfinished, the Urquiza for Paraná is unfinished, the Guirao pantheon is unfinished, and two years of his parliamentary term remain. He has run the studio at the pace of a factory for twenty years, and the work left standing in it will take other men eighteen more to finish. Rodolfo Gil is already writing the monograph; it comes out the following year and calls him a torch lit for many generations.
stops.quote: El alma de Querol es una gran antorcha encendida para muchas generaciones.
stops.quote_source: Rodolfo Gil, 'Agustín Querol', Madrid, Sáenz de Jubera Hermanos, 1910, opening pages
suggested_refs: Rodolfo Gil, Agustín Querol, Monografías de Arte Universal vol. V, Madrid, 1910

stops.name: Madrid, the Patio de San Justo
stops.date_confidence: the date of interment is not attested and the death date stands in. Contradiction unresolved: the English article names the Cementerio de San Isidro, while the Spanish article on the Cementerio de San Justo lists him by name in its Patio de San Justo. The more specific, naming source is followed
stops.campa: He is buried in the Patio de San Justo, out in Carabanchel, among the ordinary ranks of a sacramental cemetery rather than under any of the monuments he built for other men's bones. The sculptor who housed Cánovas del Castillo in eight metres of white marble, and who furnished the Panteón de Hombres Ilustres with its largest tomb, goes into the ground with nothing recorded of his own stone. Two of Madrid's cemeteries are said to hold him, and the city has never settled which.
suggested_refs: The Patio de San Justo, Cementerio de San Justo, Carabanchel, Madrid

stops.name: Madrid, the Guirao pantheon finished without him
stops.date_confidence: begun 1908, completed 1911 after his death; the cemetery coordinate is approximate for San Isidro and is not independently confirmed
stops.campa: The Guirao family pantheon at the cemetery of San Isidro, begun in his last working year, is finished two years after his death by other hands working from his drawings. It is the first of the posthumous completions. For two decades afterward his designs go on being executed by men who never met him, in Madrid, in Paraná, in Guayaquil, in Buenos Aires, each one obliged to decide what he would have meant. The studio was built to run many commissions at once, and it goes on doing that with the master dead.
suggested_refs: The Panteón Guirao, Cementerio de San Isidro, Madrid

stops.name: Paraná, the Urquiza finished by Benlliure
stops.date_confidence: inauguration attested to 1920; no month given, and the coordinate marks the Parque Urquiza generally rather than the monument's exact siting
stops.campa: Paraná, in Entre Ríos, inaugurates the equestrian monument to Justo José de Urquiza, the caudillo who broke Rosas at Caseros and gave Argentina its constitution, which Querol had begun and left standing unfinished in the studio. Mariano Benlliure completes it. The two names Spanish letters had used interchangeably for the foremost sculptor of the age end joined on a single pedestal above the Paraná river, the second man finishing the first man's horse eleven years after his death.
suggested_refs: The equestrian Monumento a Justo José de Urquiza, Parque Urquiza, Paraná

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Palermo: the gift arrives
stops.date_confidence: inaugurated 13 March 1927; attested
stops.campa: The Monumento de los Españoles is inaugurated in Palermo, seventeen years after the centenary it was meant to crown and eighteen after the death of the man who designed it. Cipriano Folgueras took it over and died in 1911. A storm broke the arm from the marble Liberty in 1914. In 1916 the steamer Príncipe de Asturias went down off the Brazilian coast carrying marble and bronze meant for the base, and the drowned pieces had to be cut a second time. The gift arrives a generation late.
suggested_refs: The wreck of the Príncipe de Asturias, 1916, with sculptural cargo bound for Buenos Aires

stops.name: Madrid, the Prado and the Querol case
stops.date_confidence: placeholder year; the sources consulted date Gaya Nuño's verdict only to the later twentieth century, and the phrase is quoted from the Spanish Wikipedia article rather than verified against the original monograph
stops.campa: The Prado holds his Sagunto and his Tradición, and the critic Juan Antonio Gaya Nuño gives the next century its verdict on him: el caso Querol, the Querol case, a reputation so far beyond the work that the age around it must have been deceived. He calls it collective psychosis, sufficient to fool nearly all of the sculptor's contemporaries and the sculptor first among them. The man who could not carve fast enough for Spain becomes, afterward, the standing example of what Spain overvalued.
stops.quote: Porque, evidentemente, hubo un caso de psicosis colectiva en derredor de este hombre suficiente para engañar a casi todos sus contemporáneos, y a él mismo a la cabeza de todos.
stops.quote_source: Juan Antonio Gaya Nuño, 'Arte del siglo XIX', as quoted in the Spanish Wikipedia article 'Agustín Querol'; not verified against the original
suggested_refs: Juan Antonio Gaya Nuño, Arte del siglo XIX, on 'el caso Querol'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Palermo: restoration and theft
stops.date_confidence: the restoration is dated 2019 to 2023 and the theft to May 2023; the day within the month is not attested and is defaulted
stops.campa: Buenos Aires restores the Monumento de los Españoles across four years, cleaning marble that a century of river air has worked on and replacing what the weather took. In May of the last of those years thieves come over the fence and cut bronze off it for the metal. The gift of the Spanish colony, already delayed by a storm, a shipwreck, and the deaths of two sculptors, goes on losing pieces of itself in the city it was given to; and the city, which has now had it far longer than Spain ever did, goes on putting them back.
suggested_refs: The 2019-2023 restoration of the Monumento de los Españoles and the May 2023 bronze theft
